articles.title_zh: Asian Stocks to Rally on US Tech Surge, Oil Slump: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Asian technology stocks surged Tuesday, tracking a rebound on Wall Street overnight as a sharp decline in oil prices lifted sentiment while renewed buying in chip names spilled over into Asia, following last week's bruising sell-off.
Japan's technology investment giant SoftBank Group surged 13.4%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest gained 2.36%. Semiconductor equipment maker Tokyo Electron rose over 4.73%, while Lasertec and Disco advanced 6.74% and 6.01%, respectively.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 5.2%, while Samsung Electronics rose 3.9%. Samsung SDI climbed 6.87%. Taiwan's TSMC added 0.45%.
China's tech-heavy ChiNext Price Index rose 1.4%.
The gains followed a strong session on Wall Street, where the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.74%, while the S&P 500 rose 2.35% to clock its best day since April 8.
The recovery came after a steep sell-off in global technology stocks last week, fueled by concerns that Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-center development, potentially impacting demand for artificial intelligence chips and infrastructure.
"This is not to suggest that the tech sell-off is done and dusted. While there is some evidence that investors are taking advantage of last week's plunge to increase their exposure to chip and other AI-adjacent stocks, there's a danger that it may be a little bit premature to load up and 'buy the dip,'" said David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation.
Beyond the political uncertainty surrounding potential restrictions on data-center development, investors have also grown increasingly wary of the enormous capital expenditures required to build out AI infrastructure. Questions over how quickly those investments will translate into meaningful profits have weighed on sentiment toward companies across the semiconductor supply chain.

U.S. stock futures largely traded near the flatline Monday night as traders awaited a pivotal consumer inflation report.
S&P 500 futures were marginally higher, while futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average were up just 18 points. Nasdaq-100 futures added 0.2%.
In Asia, South Korea's Kospi surged 4.3% Tuesday. Japan's Nikkei 225 added 2.89%, while Australia's S&P/ASX 200 gained 1.27%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index rose 0.42% and mainland's CSI 300 added 0.26%.
During the regular U.S. trading day, the Dow Industrials gained 1,104 points, or 2.2%, while the S&P 500 popped about 2.4%. The Nasdaq Composite rose 2.7%. Monday's rally came after a rocky week for markets, in which traders grew concerned of an impending slowdown in data center buildouts after Democrats posted big victories in the midterm elections.
While the tech sector rebounded in Monday's regular trading, Nvidia sat out the rally.
Shares of the chipmaker slid 4% after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials, according to The New York Times, say is a spy for China's Ministry of State Security. The company's board of directors also launched an independent internal investigation , pointing to recent reporting that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."
Oil prices also fell on Monday, lending the market support. The U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures settled down more than 4%, while Brent crude futures slid more than 5%.
Investors are awaiting the October consumer price index report due on Tuesday. Economists polled by Dow Jones see headline CPI growing at a rate of 0.3% and core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy costs, rising 0.2% from the prior month.
This would mark a deceleration from September's readings, when headline CPI grew 0.6% and core CPI advanced 0.3%.
"We think the slowdown in core CPI will stem from a reversion of shelter prices, primarily owners' equivalent rents and lodging away from home. Similarly, the stabilization in diesel prices should help to quell price pressures in energy-intensive goods," wrote Christopher Hodge, chief economist of the U.S. at Natixis CIB Americas.
Annual figures will not be provided for Tuesday's report because of the 2025 government shutdown. At that time, the Bureau of Labor Statistics was unable to collect some data which means there isn't a comparable figure for the index.
China's exports and imports surged more than expected in October, according to official data released Tuesday, while its surplus shrank sharply, undershooting estimates.
Goods exports soared by 35.2% last month from a year earlier, exceeding expectations for a 33.5% jump in a Reuters poll but slowing from the 36.3% growth in September.
Imports climbed by 41.6% last month, customs data showed, jumping from 31% in September and sharply beating Reuters-polled analysts' estimates of a 32% rise.
The trade surplus dropped to $105.3 billion in October, the lowest level since April, according to LSEG data, with year-to-date figure at $1.04 trillion, compared to a record $1.2 trillion for the full year 2025. Calls from trading partners have grown louder for Beijing to boost domestic demand and balance its economy.

The Korea Exchange activated buy-side trading curbs on both benchmark Kospi on Tuesday as the index surged over 5%.
The exchange triggered a "sidecar" mechanism, suspending program buying for five minutes. The mechanism is activated when the Kospi 200 futures index gains 5% or more for at least one minute.
The Korean index, dominated by Samsung and SK Hynix, has been seeing heightened volatility as AI plays have come under increased investor scrutiny.

Japan's Nikkei 225 added 2.78%, while the Topix rose 1.77%.

"We go around, we talk to people everywhere in this district, all we hear about is affordability on the business side, the cost,"  said he said at a Monday event in his home district. "So we've got to come to terms with this cost-side and inflation-side failure."
Goolsbee added the build-out related to artificial intelligence is also heightening the concerns.

articles.title_orig: 'Cruise for life' ship Villa Vie Odyssey seized in Singapore
articles.title_zh: 'Cruise for life' ship Villa Vie Odyssey seized in Singapore
articles.content_orig:
A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore.
The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.
Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".
The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said.
"Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".
Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.
The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.
Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.
Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website.
"For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.
However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.
While in Vietnam, crew members reportedly bought food from local grocery stores because the company owed money to a vendor who refused to deliver food, according to CBS News, the BBC's partner in the US.
CBS also reported that the operator warned passengers of its financial troubles in August, when it had sailed on a separate occasion into Singapore, and had to raise money from guests to keep the cruise going.
It had also mentioned the risk of being detained then.
Holly Hennessey, one of the ship's passengers, had earlier told the BBC guests were asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".
The vessel sailed again into Singapore earlier this month, weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end while in Cambodia.
As the Iran war sent fuel prices soaring earlier this year, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on 27 October.
It added that it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption" but those measures turned out to be insufficient to offset the "extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
The company also said it was working with residents to "identify temporary living arrangements" while in Cambodia.

articles.title_orig: After meeting Qatar PM, Trump calls Iran war ‘effectively over’ militarily
articles.title_zh: After meeting Qatar PM, Trump calls Iran war ‘effectively over’ militarily
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump has signalled that he considers the US-Israel war on Iran “effectively” at an end, after meeting Qatar’s prime minister in Washington, DC.
In a surprise briefing on Monday, Trump reiterated his position that the US had destroyed Iran’s military. But his remarks suggested he faces pressure from allies in the Middle East to bring hostilities to a close.
“Iran militarily is effectively over,” he said. “We’re just keeping it the status quo, and we’re doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours.”
His comments followed a closed-door meeting with US Vice President JD Vance and Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, who hailed the progress in a post on social media.
“We discussed the situation in the region and ways to progress the US-Iran talks,” the prime minister said. “Grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region.”
Still, Trump acknowledged the “status quo” would involve continuing the US naval blockade against Iranian ports, as well as the newly announced Task Force Iron Gate, which seeks to cut off trade by land and through the Caspian Sea.
“Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and others would prefer the status quo, that we remain as is,” he said. “In other words, a continuation of the greatest naval blockade in the history of our country. Probably in the history of the world.”
Trump also indicated in his briefing that the US was willing to resume fighting, should the need arise.
“Taking military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing, but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes,” he said.
“Israel and the entire Middle East are protected from Iranian danger and threats, and we’re seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it’s going to be ending fairly soon.”
Iranian officials, meanwhile, dismissed Trump’s latest remarks as a distraction.
“The war on Iran has already wrecked the US government. But Washington flails like a desperate gambler,” Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei wrote in a post on social media.
“FOLD YOUR HAND. STOP manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks.”
Separately, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said that the country’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had called for an end to the situation, which he described as “neither war nor peace”.
Pezeshkian added that Iran was open to further negotiations but would not be coerced, according to Iranian media. “We will not surrender to force and bullying,” he said.
Since the war on Iran began on February 28, the conflict has spilled into surrounding countries and roiled international trade.
Almost as soon as the US and Israel began their attacks, Iran moved to shut down the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for oil, gas and fertiliser, among other goods.
Iran also responded to US and Israeli strikes with missile and drone fire on its neighbours in the Gulf, including Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE, with many of the attacks targeting US military installations.
Other, related conflicts have since emerged. Saudi Arabia has renewed its fight against the Iran-backed Houthis, and Israel began its occupation of southern Lebanon, as well as deadly air strikes.
In the nearly nine months since the war began, the US offensive against Iran has grown sporadic, with intermittent exchanges of fire.
In recent days, for instance, the Trump administration announced “minor strikes” against Iran’s Qeshm Island.
It also offered a $20m reward for “information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel”.
After the Twelve-Day War in June 2025, Trump had claimed that Iran’s uranium enrichment programme had been obliterated. But he has since made curtailing Iran’s nuclear programme a central premise for the ongoing war.
Iran has long denied seeking a nuclear weapon, maintaining its uranium enrichment programme is for the purposes of civilian energy generation.
Officials in Iran, meanwhile, have pushed for the US to accept seven conditions in order to end the war.
They include lifting US sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian funds, recognising a new shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz worked out with Oman, and ending the war on all fronts, including Israel’s attacks on Lebanon.
Qatar has served as one of several key mediators in the conflict. Sheikh Mohammed, the prime minister, also serves as foreign minister and has been known to act as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran.
In Monday’s closed-door meeting, he reportedly presented Trump with a two-day proposal from Iran to end the war.
Afterwards, reporters asked Trump in the briefing room, “Why not just declare an end to the conflict and be done with it?”
Trump replied by framing the continued US blockade as a question of regional security. He also called for a “long-term solution”, rather than a short-term one.
“We have some great allies there, and we have to make sure they’re not hurt, and they would be hurt,” he said.
“They are right now a lot safer than they were six months ago because Iran’s been very much decapitated. But they’re still the bully of the Middle East a little bit.”

"The only thing that matters the rest of this year is the Anthropic IPO," said Neostellar principal Willy Lee on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang. Lee said investors want to know whether Anthropic can sustain long-term growth and secure a meaningful share of the AI market.
"Those are the two questions that every investor is asking within their investment committee every single day before the IPO," said Lee.
Anthropic recently revealed revenue grew $1,206% to $33.2 billion through the first nine months of the year. The company also noted a staggering aggregate committed spend of $895.4 billion , which it says is primarily related to compute and infrastructure.
But the AI growth story was put to the test this past week as investors weighed a Democratic congressional win against the impact of the AI data center build-out. On Thursday, the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) suffered its worst daily decline since April 2025, with chip stocks leading the declines.
The market turmoil prompted prospective buyers to discuss lowering Anthropic's valuation to a range of $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion, with some considering as low as $1.1 trillion, according to Bloomberg. That's far below estimates as high as $2 trillion projected in early October.
Amid increasingly jittery sentiment toward AI stocks, Anthropic faces a difficult decision, particularly if the unwinding of the AI trade continues.
"It would be difficult to go public," Anna Rathbun, founder and CEO of Grenadilla Advisory, told Yahoo Finance's Market Hang.
If Anthropic decides to delay its IPO, investors could interpret the move as a bearish signal for the AI trade, said Kevin Mahn, chief investment officer at Hennion & Walsh.
"If they don't delay, and their IPO fails, or comes in below expectations, that could be perceived as bearish to certain investors," said Mahn. "Damned if you do, damned if you don't."
Investors will also be looking for clues about the health of the AI trade on Nov. 17, when Nvidia ( NVDA ) reports earnings. With hyperscalers Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Amazon ( AMZN ), and Meta ( META ) having already reported, along with foundry Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM ) and chip equipment maker ASML ( ASML ), expectations are high that Nvidia will once again beat earnings estimates and raise its guidance.
"We got so much confirmation already," said Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum. "I give it a 1% chance that they miss."

articles.title_orig: Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang amid allegations he was target of Chinese intelligence effort
articles.title_zh: Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang amid allegations he was target of Chinese intelligence effort
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia has launched an independent investigation of its co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang , over allegations he was the target of an intelligence effort by China.
The allegations center around a Chinese business executive named Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was an asset of China's Ministry of State Security , the country's main intelligence agency.
The CIA, NSA and ODNI did not immediately respond to CBS News requests for comment.
The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities were investigating Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen), a former executive of the Singapore-based Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia . The report claims Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security.
Two law enforcement sources confirmed to CBS News on Monday that the Justice Department's National Security Division is investigating Megaspeed. The investigation involves potential violations of U.S. export restrictions on advanced AI chips, the sources said.
In a message to Nvidia employees Sunday, Jensen Huang admitted, "I was unfaithful to my wife," and apologized for hurting her and their children, although he did not name the woman involved. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote.
"The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," Nvidia's board of directors said in a statement Sunday. "A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."
The board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," the statement said.
John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, told CBS News on Sunday, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."
Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters Monday, "The so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear."
A company spokesperson said Jensen Huang "fully supports the review" and is committed to continuing to lead the company.
Jensen Huang said he had fallen short of his responsibilities to the company's employees, board and shareholders. He said he is "fully committed to NVIDIA" and will work to earn back their trust.
"Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation," he said in a statement. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully."
"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," he added.
Alice Huang was previously a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to The Times.
Asked about the report on Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he couldn't comment, saying it was an "internal corporate matter."
On Monday, President Trump called Jensen Huang a "very high-quality person," saying during a White House briefing that "the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape." Mr. Trump also said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday to see how he was doing, and that Huang "said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy."
Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, has regularly surpassed Wall Street's earnings expectations in the past three years since its high-end chips emerged as AI's best building blocks. The Santa Clara, California-based company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion in August.
Nicole  Sganga , Olivia  Gazis and The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: M. John Harrison’s ‘The End of Everything’ Wins Booker Prize
articles.title_zh: M. John Harrison’s ‘The End of Everything’ Wins Booker Prize
articles.content_orig:
The British author M. John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize, considered one of the most prestigious literary awards for a work of fiction. At 81 years old, he is also the oldest author ever to be awarded with the honor.
The announcement was made during a ceremony at London’s Old Billingsgate, the site of a former fish market, on Monday. Harrison will receive a prize of £50,000 ($67,000). This year’s judging panel, chaired by historian Mary Beard, featured writers Raymond Antrobus and Patricia Lockwood, critic Rebecca Liu and musician Jarvis Cocker, front man of the British band Pulp.
Harrison’s post-apocalyptic turn, titled “The End of Everything,” takes place in the English coastal town of Dalston-on-Sea in the not-too-distant future, during the occupation of mysterious lifeforms called the iGhetti. Though much about the visitors’ origins remains ambiguous, the author told BBC radio that the real-world event that sparked the plot was the 2008 financial crisis. At 198 pages, it was the slimmest of the six shortlisted books.
“‘The End of Everything’” can be read as a thriller, a mystery, a satire, a dystopia, a road novel, a work of realism; whatever the reader is looking for can be found here, albeit told at a slant and with a twist,” the jury wrote in a Q&A published ahead of the announcement.
Harrison’s win could be considered the first time a science fiction novel has been awarded the prize. Though the 2024 winner “Orbital” takes place aboard a space station, the philosophical novel is murkier in its categorization. Regardless, this year marks a rare recognition of the genre and honors an author who has published within it for more than five decades. Harrison began his “Virconium” series in 1971, set on a futuristic Earth, and continued writing about the fictional city in novels and stories through 1984. Among his other works, he completed the “Kefahuchi Tract” trilogy between 2002 and 2012. This year was the first time he was nominated for the Booker Prize.
“You talk glibly about your life being changed, but it’s weird when it happens. I feel like a proper writer at last, totally lacking in confidence,” Harrison said as he accepted the award.
Harrison beat five other finalists, including the betting market’s favorites Marlon James and Douglas Stuart, both former winners.
Harrison was selected from 163 submissions that were narrowed down to a 13-book longlist and six finalists, announced in September. The shortlist included James “The Disappearers” and Stuart’s “John of John” as well as Luke Kennard’s “Black Bag,” Elizabeth Strout’s “The Things We Never Say,” and Rebecca Perry’s “May We Feed the King.”
Doomscrolling (and kids) destroyed my reading habit. Could the ‘Booker Challenge’ save it?
Ahead of Monday’s ceremony, the Booker Prize Foundation’s chief executive, Gaby Wood, said that the shortlisted books were unified by a question: “What can we know of each other, what do we infer or assume, what are we prepared to see?”
“Despite the great range in their styles and subjects, in all of these novels we find forms of isolation: relationships breaking down or withheld, people harboring secrets or pain, characters closing themselves off from others or attempting to reach beyond their solitude towards them,” Wood said, according to a statement on the Prize’s official website.
First awarded in 1969, the Booker Prize was originally only open to writers from the UK, Ireland or Commonwealth nations. From the 2014 prize onwards, eligibility was opened to include English-language authors of any nationality, as long as the nominated work is published in the UK or Irish markets. Its sister award, the International Booker Prize, is meanwhile awarded for a work of fiction that has been translated into English.
Last year’s Booker Prize went to author David Szalay’s “Flesh,” a sparsely written novel recounting a taciturn Hungarian immigrant’s journey from poverty to the upper echelons of London high society. Other notable winners include Salman Rushdie, William Golding, Ian McEwan, Arundhati Roy and Kazuo Ishiguro. Margaret Atwood previously held the distinction of the oldest author to be honored, when she was jointly recognized at age 79 for “The Testaments.” She shared the 2019 Booker Prize with Bernardine Evaristo, author of “Girl, Woman, Other.”

articles.content_orig:
Sign up to get our news digest — delivered directly to your inbox twice a week.
Disney has lined up its next big AI partner, this time teaming with Adobe on a multi-year alliance to bring customized generative AI models into its creative pipelines across its businesses, including tools that will transform hand-drawn sketches into fully rendered concept art.
Under the terms of the agreement, Adobe will be Disney’s official “AI Innovation Partner” and will give the company access to Firefly, Firefly Foundry, Premiere, Photoshop, and dedicated engineering resources. Together, the companies will develop bespoke AI models trained on Disney IP to “generate commercially safe and production-ready outputs.”
According to the release , the work is already underway, with Walt Disney Imagineering using Firefly Foundry to generate 2D concept art from human-made drawings and create IP-based graphics for its parks development. Adobe will also work with Disney’s StudioLAB on experimental production workflows and ESPN Edge on AI-powered sports content.
The Adobe partnership is only the latest in a string of high-profile attempts by Disney to get ahead of the AI curve through corporate partnerships.
A year ago, Disney unveiled its most dramatic overhaul of Disney+ since the streamer’s launch, including a full-on embrace of generative AI tools for users. Then, in December, the company announced a $1 billion investment in OpenAI, a deal that collapsed when Sora was shut down and before any money changed hands.
More recently, Disney hired former Character.AI CEO Karandeep Anand as its first chief technology officer and committed roughly $180 million to recruiting employees from his former company, as it announced another major round of layoffs in a year largely defined by cuts across the company.
While the financial terms of the Adobe deal have not been made public, such a high-profile partnership once again shows where Disney’s priorities lie. Even as it eliminates thousands of jobs, demands further cost reductions, and commits billions to shareholder-benefiting stock buybacks, the company continues pouring resources into AI technologies that could fundamentally change how creative work is produced, and who gets paid to do it.

articles.title_orig: White House cautiously upbeat about Russia-Ukraine peace talks this week
articles.title_zh: White House cautiously upbeat about Russia-Ukraine peace talks this week
articles.content_orig:
A fresh round of peace talks between the US, Ukraine and Russia are set to begin Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, as the Trump administration renews its drive to end the nearly five-year conflict even after it announced significant concessions to Moscow.
Russia has made clear it wants the negotiations – the first of their kind since February – to be strictly trilateral, though national security advisers from several European nations, as well as officials from NATO and the European Union, are also expected in the UAE capital for separate meetings.
“We are working hard to find a negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine,” US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and US negotiator Jared Kushner said Monday.
US officials on Monday underlined that posture, saying that the upcoming talks are a new starting point in defining an end to the war, including discussions on security guarantees and a “post-war security architecture.”
“We need to come up with a way that, when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war, and we believe that’s what Ukraine wants. We believe that’s what Europe wants and we believe that’s what Russia wants,” one official said.
However, many – particularly in Europe – have cast doubt on Moscow’s intentions. The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said Monday she saw little sign that Russia was willing to negotiate in good faith.
Meanwhile, the US official also said that it would be up to Trump to decide whether to offer a US security guarantee as part of peace talks.
The US will be represented by Kushner and Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff, while Ukraine’s foreign intelligence chief and top negotiator Rustem Umerov will lead the Ukrainian delegation, according to the official with knowledge of the talks.
Russia is sending deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin as delegates, according to Russian state news agency TASS, as well as Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and member of general staff Yuri Zhigarlovsky.
Representatives from the E4 group – the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Italy – as well as officials from NATO and the European Commission will also be in Abu Dhabi, Umerov said Monday. “We will hold separate coordination meetings with our European partners,” Umerov added.
Asked about the presence of European officials in Abu Dhabi, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that Europe has its own channels of communication with Kyiv and Washington, while reaffirming that the talks are “a trilateral negotiation – involving Russia and Ukraine – with the United States acting as a mediator.”
Notably, these talks come amid a renewed push by European nations for a more active role in negotiations over Ukraine’s future, and the security of the bloc at large, after Trump touted a new security deal for Ukraine that “might involve all of Europe.”
“The Europeans will be well represented,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told French media Sunday. “In recent weeks, the Europeans have made their voices heard. They have expressed to the American mediator that no discussion affecting the future of the continent can ignore our expectations and demands,” he added.
Europe has long been wary of any US-brokered peace deal negotiated without its involvement, with Umerov saying Monday that Ukraine was “doing everything we can to ensure that Europe is a participant in the diplomatic process.”
While the talks will remain trilateral, Kushner said that he and Witkoff would also meet with European partners to continue the “close consultation and coordination we have undertaken on European security and Ukraine’s postwar future over the past several weeks.”
“Ultimately, achieving a comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them,” Kushner posted on X.
This will be the fourth round of trilateral talks. All have ended without significant breakthrough.
Earlier this year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the most recent trilateral talks in Geneva, Switzerland, in February fell short of Ukraine’s goals, saying “sensitive political matters, issues of possible compromises and the necessary meeting of leaders have not yet been sufficiently worked through.”
The US later postponed a round of trilateral talks that were expected to take place in March due to the war in Iran.
Putin is still making maximalist demands previously rejected by Kyiv, including Russian control over Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, a reduction in the size of Ukraine’s military and the abandonment of Kyiv’s ambitions to join NATO.
John Herbst, senior director of the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center and a former US ambassador to Ukraine, said any expectations for the Abu Dhabi talks should be “very modest.”
“They are only taking place because Putin wants to give Trump a reason to continue to distance himself from Ukraine,” Herbst wrote last week .
With Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year and gains on the battlefield remaining difficult to come by, Moscow has escalated its aerial attacks – with deadly results for Ukrainians.
At least 55 people were killed last Monday when Russia dropped several bombs on a school building used as a shelter and aid center in Zaporizhzhia , marking one of the deadliest single incidents of the war to date. Civilian deaths in Ukraine are at their highest point since the start of the war, with more than 2,700 killed in Russian strikes so far this year, according to ACLED, a global conflict monitor.
And continuing a pattern seen in previous years, Russian drones and missiles are already hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, but harder and earlier than in other winters, analysts say. Russian attacks on the power grid left more than 600,000 people in the Dnipropetrovsk region without electricity overnight into Sunday, Zelensky said, as temperatures plummet and winter draws in.
Over the past few months, Russia has deployed faster, jet-powered Shahed drones, which are harder to shoot down. At the same time, more missiles are slipping through Ukraine’s air defenses as Kyiv grapples with a chronic shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors that are one of the few defensive weapons capable of shooting down ballistic missiles.
Where the Biden administration positioned the US as Ukraine’s biggest single donor and most powerful ally, the Trump administration’s relationship with Kyiv has been decidedly more complicated. It halted financial aid to Ukraine at the beginning of 2025, while the intelligence and technology support it still provides has come under strain in recent weeks too.
Last month, Zelensky accused his Western allies of not providing intelligence warnings before multiple ballistic missile attacks, a claim that the Trump administration denied.
In October too, Ukraine’s ability to use Starshield, a military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink service that is critical to its military operations, was hampered when speed limits were imposed on the satellite terminals. Trump denied approving that decision, while Musk said the Trump administration was behind the ban in a social media post.
Undergirding all this recent tension has been Trump’s sensitivity to rising gas prices, which skyrocketed due to the Iran war and contributed to the Republicans’ landslide defeat in last week’s midterms.
He has shown a willingness to strike business deals with Moscow, including one to supply markets with Russia’s diesel, in a sharp break from the sanctions aimed at punishing and isolating the Russian economy, and pressured Zelensky to accept a short-lived “energy ceasefire.”

articles.content_orig:
Johnny Doughnuts , a Food Network favorite that has expanded across the Bay Area over the past decade , will close three of its six locations on Tuesday, Nov. 10, including its Santa Rosa shop.
In addition to the Santa Rosa shop at 1200 4th Street, the doughnut brand shut down operations at its Pacific Heights location in San Francisco and Santana Row in San Jose, laying off 34 employees. Johnny Doughnuts locations in Napa’s Oxbow Public Market, Larkspur’s Marin Country Mart, and its flagship store in San Rafael will remain open.
“Today (Monday), Johnny Doughnuts announced it is closing three of its six locations so it can focus on its core shops,” Sara Segal, a spokesperson for the company, told The Press Democrat, noting that the remaining stores will be “operating as usual, and catering and events” will continue as planned.
Segal said that no additional layoffs are being considered at this time for those three remaining locations.
Co-founders Craig Blum and Kim Diamond launched Johnny Doughnuts in 2012 as a food truck operating across the Bay Area before opening their first brick-and-mortar storefront a year later in the West End Village neighborhood of San Rafael.
Known for a menu that includes vegan and wheat-free options, Johnny Doughnuts began expanding in 2017 with a location in Hayes Valley, San Francisco. That shop closed in 2022 and relocated to Pacific Heights on Fillmore Street, which ultimately will close on Tuesday.
In 2019, Johnny Doughnuts opened its shop in Marin County, followed by expansions into Sonoma and Napa counties between 2021 and 2026.The closing San Jose location had just opened this past summer at Santana Row , an upscale open-air shopping center.
Johnny Doughnuts was featured and ranked among the nation’s top five doughnut shops on the Food Network in 2015, and was selected by Press Democrat readers for the Best of Sonoma County list in 2022 and 2023.
According to the company’s website, Blum began crafting doughnuts “using high-quality, locally sourced ingredients and a touch of nostalgia,” relying on recipes inspired by “classic 1920s techniques” that incorporate fresh potatoes to achieve a unique texture.
Segal added that Johnny Doughnuts is “deeply grateful” to its employees, customers, and partners, and that the company is committed to “supporting the team members affected by these closures.”
Customers with questions can contact the company at connect@johnnydoughnuts.com .

Friday's market partially rebounded from Thursday's brutal artificial intelligence-driven sell-off, as chip stocks recovered on renewed buying. However, concerns linger in the wake of the Democrats' strong midterm results, with investors fearing that tighter regulations on data center construction, energy use, and development costs could slow the AI infrastructure boom .
The tech sector also focused on the bombshell announcement Sunday that Nvidia's board of directors is opening an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who U.S. intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. Nvidia shares closed down 4%.
"Magnificent Seven" names were higher contrary to Nvidia. Amazon gained about 3%, while Tesla and Alphabet climbed 5.5% and 1%, respectively. Microsoft also added almost 3%.
Other chip stocks advanced as well, with Broadcom popping nearly 9% and Advanced Micro Devices jumping 13%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) — which dropped around 13% last week — rose more than 7%.

"There are still a lot of overhangs on the market," the CEO said, pointing to elevated oil prices as a result of the Middle East conflict as well as the Federal Reserve's interest rate outlook.
This week , investors are looking ahead to key AI-related earnings — CoreWeave , Cisco and Applied Materials are all on deck — as they assess the outlook for tech and whether the recent sell-off has further to run.

articles.content_orig:
New leaks reveal the camera specs for Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series which includes three lenses across the lineup, but not the upgrades you want, nor what Ultra owners might expect.
SammyGuru reports that Samsung is “evaluating” camera setups for the Galaxy S27, S27+, S27 Pro, and S27 Ultra, and it looks like a mixed bag across the board.
The base Galaxy S27 and S27+ are looking very familiar, with identical main camera sensors to last year, and the same ultrawide sensor that’s been in use since the Galaxy S23 series. The telephoto and selfie sensors are looking at new hardware, but without any major spec upgrades.
Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, meanwhile, have a new 200MP main camera on deck, a 50MP ultrawide shooter, and a mere 12MP telephoto. The Ultra might get 5x compared to the Pro’s 3x optical zoom, but with a secondary telephoto lens going missing, existing users of the lineup are sure to be disappointed.
Notably, SammyGuru’s article mentions the Pro as using “the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s 3x sensor,” but shows the 12MP Samsung S5K3LD in that place instead. We’re assuming that’s a typo seeing as the post mentions the Pro as using the Samsung S5KJN3 or the Sony IMX855 earlier on, but regardless, the Pro only gets 3x optical zoom to the Ultra’s 5x.
Some of these specs have been mentioned by other sources such as GalaxyClub and leaker Ice Universe , but this is the most complete picture of the S27’s camera plans we’ve seen to date.
Personally, I’m very “whelmed” on this one. As RAMageddon rages on and Samsung hunts for new ways to balance specs vs price, cameras are a place that’s obviously going to be cut, but competitors are already running laps around Samsung on the hardware front. Cutting lenses and skimping out on upgrades ( again ) doesn’t help matters.

articles.title_orig: Silicon Valley’s Trump-era playbook is falling apart. A major shift is underway.
articles.title_zh: Silicon Valley’s Trump-era playbook is falling apart. A major shift is underway.
articles.content_orig:
Democrats won seats on anti-datacentre tickets and Musk wasted nearly half a billion dollars. Big tech may be losing its grip, but it won’t go quietly
P hotos That Precede Unfortunate Events: a couple of months back, Donald Trump hosted some of the world’s most powerful tech executives at the White House for a “ Super Intelligence luncheon ”, which by coincidence is also how my mum described her tuna sandwiches in a forlorn attempt to get me to eat them. Sitting either side of the president were Elon Musk, making a rare offline appearance in daylight hours, and Jensen Huang, the Nvidia chief executive carving out a precious slot in what we now know was an extremely busy schedule.
Over a delicious meal of microchips and rare-earth metals, the billionaires sketched out a utopian future of an AI industry unencumbered by regulation or safeguards, powered by their heroic strongman leader, a political genius effortlessly able to impose his will upon an entire nation. And perhaps it should have been apparent even at the time that these (mostly) men were putting their faith in a guy who had recently been defeated by pond algae . But as the drinks and the good times flowed, it was still possible to believe that the sun would never set on the thousand-year American superintelligence empire.
And so, while we’re all learning lessons from the resounding defeat delivered to Trumpism last week, might we start with a modest and sober reassessment of the Silicon Valley oligarch class? For years, we have been told that these are some of humanity’s greatest seers and visionaries, the Leonardos and Einsteins of the 21st century, the people best placed to plot a course for our species, despite for the most part not being able to smile without looking as though they were undergoing a juice enema.
As it turned out, this small band of brilliant clairvoyants somehow failed to anticipate the possibility that the deeply unpopular man they were clasping in a tender embrace would be subjected to an absolute democracy-mogging in just a few weeks, throwing their altruistic wet dreams into chaos. After all, last week’s midterms were not simply a rebuke to one man or one party, but to an entire ideology. Across the US, voters took their revenge not just on big tech, but on the politicians who had enabled it.
In Texas, Gina Hinojosa beat the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott, by promising an immediate moratorium on datacentre development, and despite being outspent almost eight to one, in large part by big tech donors desperate to preserve their tax breaks. In Ohio, the Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown described his opponent, Jon Husted, as “the face of datacentres”, a visually horrifying concept. In total, 46 of the 47 ballot measures relating to datacentres were defeated . By Thursday morning, the markets had responded with a devastating sell-off of tech stocks , the repercussions of which are still shaking out as you read this.
Should we read anything into the fact that the biggest progressive landslide in 52 years, catalysed by a concerted mobilisation of Black, Latino and young voters, was sufficient to send the financial markets into existential panic? Anyone able to join the dots for us there? Is it relevant that the São Paulo stock exchange plunged about 14% after Lula da Silva’s shock election victory in Brazil last month? Just what is it about the popular repudiation of hard-right autocrats that appears to spook the pillars of capitalism so much?
For the time being, big tech does not appear to be as politically polarising in Britain as it is in the US. This is largely because much of the recent acceleration has occurred under a Labour administration, in particular under the late lamented Keir Starmer, a prime minister who in retrospect may actually have been a semi-sentient chatbot all along. “We will test and understand AI before we regulate it,” Starmer once said, which he appears to have done by plugging it directly into his own mouth for two years. But this is an issue that will continue to rise in democratic salience, in part because it relies on the undemocratic manufacture of consent, an inexorable march deliberately designed to circumvent scrutiny.
after newsletter promotion
Take the UK government’s AI growth zones , designed to supercharge datacentre development by taking decisions on nationally significant infrastructure projects (NSIP) away from local councils. A recent report by Spotlight on Corruption found that over two years, ministers met only two community groups and no environmental organisations while developing the policy, while at the same time ministers and senior civil servants were hired to 38 roles at AI companies. Naturally, you are likely to hear very little opposition to any of this, either from the billionaire-owned press or the official opposition; indeed, Kemi Badenoch is perhaps the only major party leader you can imagine typing “what do I think of AI” into an AI prompt.
You will occasionally hear the assumption, made on both sides of the Atlantic and often on the flimsiest of evidence, that voters are increasingly fed up with democracy. But what if we’re getting this the wrong way round? What if, in fact, it is those who are supposed to be upholding democracy – the politicians and media and captains of industry, all slowly stewing in X-brained algorithmic talking points – who are beginning to tire of it? While Musk spends enormous chunks of his fortune trying (and failing) to tip the electoral scales in favour of the hard right, Reform UK rakes in £72m in donations from two cryptocurrency billionaires. Bonus question: do we think the brave men and women out there on the tech frontier will respond to democratic setbacks by demanding more democratic accountability, or less?
And, of course, in these febrile and fragile times you have to take your wins wherever you get them. But as any ChatGPT user will tell you, making bold claims on the basis of a bare minimum of data is always an exercise fraught with risk. Saying no once will never be enough. In a note to investors last week, Goldman Sachs wrote: “We expect the datacentre issue to somewhat fade in importance and any moratoria on datacentre development to be short-lived.” You can decide for yourself what it means by that.

articles.title_orig: Trump Media cashes in on high-speed access to social media posts
articles.title_zh: Trump Media cashes in on high-speed access to social media posts
articles.content_orig:
Trump Media and Technology Group reported Monday that revenue surged 205% in the third quarter, which it says was “primarily driven” by selling a high-speed feed of posts on Truth Social.
The “Truth API,” as the company calls it, allows news organizations, Wall Street trading firms and other services to pay $60,000 to $100,000 per month for a direct feed of posts on the social network. Critics have slammed the feed as an attempt to profit from President Donald Trump’s posts.
Trump, whose revocable trust is the largest single shareholder of Trump Media, is the most prominent user of Truth Social.
Trump’s trust owns more than 41% of Trump Media, according to S&P Capital IQ data. In a June filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the trust said Donald Trump Jr. was “the sole trustee and has sole voting and investment power” over its holdings.
Trump Media’s stock, which trades under the symbol DJT for Trump’s initials, closed at $4.06 on Monday, giving it a market valuation of $1.13 billion. It’s down 69% so far this year.
In July, Trump Media announced the high-speed feed offering , saying it would allow “real-time access to posts from the highest-ranking Truth Social accounts.”
The company acknowledged that the service could be market-moving and highly valuable to any trading firm.
“Markets already move on Truth Social posts,” Kevin McGurn, interim CEO of Trump Media, said at the time. He added that “high frequency and algorithmic trading firms that require a low-latency, machine-readable feed rather than manual tracking” could benefit from paying for the feed.
In August, the company said the service had gone live.
Last month, Reuters reported that Bloomberg and two Wall Street trading firms were some of the customers who had signed up for the service. Bloomberg declined to comment to NBC News in October, while the two other firms did not reply to requests for comment at the time.
Two top Democratic senators, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Adam Schiff of California, said the Truth Social feed amounts to “an outrageous abuse of the President’s office for his personal benefit.” In July, they asked the SEC to “determine whether the proposed arrangement would violate applicable federal securities laws.”
Trump was asked Sunday whether he was using the presidency to enrich himself.
“I devote almost no time to my net worth,” Trump told CBS News’ “60 Minutes” in an interview. “I have a lot of money, and far more than I ever thought I’d have. And I guess it’s gone up. I don’t even know.”
Trump said his son “watches over” his money, adding: “I don’t even talk to him about it.”
Trump’s personal finances differ vastly from those of other recent presidents. In June, Trump’s most recent personal financial disclosure ran more than 900 pages . By comparison, President Barack Obama’s final disclosure form was eight pages, while President Joe Biden’s was 11. Vice President JD Vance’s form for last year is 17 pages.
Trump’s disclosure shows billions of dollars in earnings tied to cryptocurrencies, media settlements and vast personal investments in stocks and bonds.
The White House has repeatedly insisted that “neither the President nor his family has ever engaged — or will ever engage — in conflicts of interest.”
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Man who sent racist threats to UK Conservative leader Badenoch receives jail sentence
articles.title_zh: Man who sent racist threats to UK Conservative leader Badenoch receives jail sentence
articles.content_orig:
A man has been jailed for sending the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch emails threatening to shoot her dead.
Ex-teacher Kieran Kyle sent three emails on 2 May to the Tory party leader in which he made racist references and claimed to have been in the IRA, the court heard.
The 43-year-old, from Gillingham in Kent, pleaded guilty on 22 September at Westminster Magistrates' Court to two counts of sending communications of an indecent or offensive nature.
Kyle was sentenced to 20 weeks in prison at the same court on Monday.
In a victim impact statement read to the court, Badenoch and her husband Hamish said the "malicious communications and targeted harassment" not only had an effect on them, but also undermined "a healthy democracy".
In two of the emails, Kyle had made racist references and written: "I'm ex-IRA, so Bloody Sunday references from you are going to give you trouble," the court heard.
The messages were sent on the day Badenoch apologised for footage from Bloody Sunday being mistakenly used in a social media clip to criticise a parliamentary Bill on legacy issues in Northern Ireland.
The Tory leader had said she did not sign off the video and that it was sent out by "very young people".
The video criticising the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, posted to her social media channels on 28 April, showed Badenoch saying the Labour legislation would "drag" Troubles veterans back to court.
Thirteen unarmed civilians were shot dead when members of the Army's Parachute Regiment opened fire on civil rights demonstrators in the Bogside area of Londonderry on 30 January 1972, a date that became known as Bloody Sunday.
The court heard Kyle had also sent an email to Badenoch's husband Hamish on 29 April, which used a racist term and said she had a "big mouth" and he should "put a leash on her".
Prosecutor Ben Holt said the North West Essex MP and her husband were left "distressed" and "upset", particularly by the "racist language and threats of violence used towards them".
He added Cheryl Bacon, head of Badenoch's parliamentary office, said the emails were "disgusting" and "distressing" to read.
Baiju Thittala, defending, told the court Kyle "did not know" who Badenoch was at the time of the offences, adding "he only realised later, once he had sent the emails".
Asked by the judge how Kyle, a former secondary school teacher, could not know who Badenoch was, Thittala said: "He just 'Googled' it and it came up as the opposition leader."
The judge said: "The first emails were sent to Mr Badenoch, so I don't think he did not appreciate who Mrs Badenoch was.
"So he clearly knew who Mrs Badenoch was because he researched her husband's details first."
The Badenochs said in their victim impact statement: "Our primary concern arising from this offence is not the personal impact on us, but the wider consequences that malicious communications and targeted harassment have on our democratic life.
"When individuals choose to intimidate, threaten, or aggressively target elected representatives or public figures, the harm extends far beyond any single person. It undermines a healthy democracy."
The continued: "Public service relies on people being willing to step forward, often at significant personal cost, to represent their communities and contribute to public life.
"Increasingly, however, those who do so face hostility, harassment, and attempts to silence or intimidate them."
The judge also handed Kyle a restraining order, meaning he cannot contact Badenoch, her husband or her parliamentary office for five years.

Six months before the Nvidia spy scandal emerged , the New York-based short seller firm Culper Research had already raised questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unusually close relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips. She is now suspected to be a Chinese spy.
The Nvidia CEO admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and the company has now opened a formal investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang (who shares his last name but is not related). U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.
Culper’s May 13 report is resurfacing because it picked up on the connection between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang while investigating Megaspeed’s ties to Nvidia.

In particular, the report called the relationship between the two executives “uncomfortably close,” noting that the Nvidia CEO was spotted partying and socializing with Alice Huang on multiple occasions. The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.”
Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies. It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source.
Financial Times reported Monday that documents show Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries.
Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. Its report is available on the web and was posted to X back in May .

articles.title_orig: Security Levels At U.S. Bases In England Raised Without Explanation
articles.title_zh: Security Levels At U.S. Bases In England Raised Without Explanation
articles.content_orig:
At least two bases in England hosting U.S. Air Force aircraft are operating under beefed-up security protocols, a U.S. official told us Monday afternoon. The official was responding to our questions about what appeared to be unusual aircraft movements out of RAF Mildenhall. It is unclear what spurred these measures, how long they have been in place or whether they are connected to an ongoing investigation into whether Iran was behind a security incident at RAF Fairford in September that reportedly prompted the hasty departure of B-1 Lancer bombers.
“Enhanced force protection measures are in effect across RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall,” the official told us. “We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families. We are working closely with our host nation counterparts to minimize impacts from enhanced force protection activities and ensure the safety of U.S. personnel, their families and the local community.”
The official declined to say what steps were taken.
“For operational security reasons, we do not discuss specific force protection measures,” the official added.
RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath are both major hubs for the U.S. Air Force. Mildenhall’s host unit is the 100th Air Refueling Wing, which operates KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refueling jets. The base is also home to Air Force RC-135V/W Rivet Joint reconnaissance aircraft , Air Force Special Operations Command (AFSOC) CV-22 Osprey tiltrotor aircraft and MC-130J Commando II special operations cargo planes . Lakenheath hosts Air Force F-15E Strike Eagle and F-35A Lightning II aircraft .
Both bases also see frequent flights transiting to other locations.
As we noted earlier in this piece, the official was responding to our questions about unusual aircraft movements out of Mildenhall. They were first noticed by the @DefenceGeek open-source flight tracker account.
“Over the course of today, a number of US Air Force assets at RAF Mildenhall (EGUN) have made unannounced/unexpected movements to other locations, with several of those movements in motion presently,” DefenceGeek wrote on X. “The initial few this morning I assumed were due to heavy fog in the area, but other information is now suggesting something else… – Several KC-135s have moved to Spangdahlem (ETAD) or Prestwick (EGPK) – CV-22Bs have moved from Mildenhall to Lakenheath It remains unclear if there is an ongoing exercise or information of a potential threat (following the incident at RAF Fairford)…”
UPDATE: US Assets at RAF Mildenhall Dispersing For those commenting and asking, no, the NOTAMs regarding RAF Mildenhall are not related to what is currently going on. The two NOTAMs are for Veterans Day (Wednesday) and Thanksgiving (end of November). Today's situation does not…
DefenceGeek also noted that RAF Lakenheath posted a notice this morning on Facebook urging vigilance in spotting and reporting drones.
US Assets at RAF Mildenhall Dispersing? Over the course of today, a number of US Air Force assets at RAF Mildenhall (EGUN) have made unannounced/unexpected movements to other locations, with several of those movements in motion presently. The initial few this morning I assumed… pic.twitter.com/vVVA0cRljN
“Our strongest security asset is an observant community,” the RAF Lakenheath Facebook post read . “Staying vigilant and reporting suspicious activity, including unauthorized drone activity, helps protect our Airmen, families and mission. If you see something unusual on or around the Tri-Base area, report it to Security Forces.”
It is unclear what connection, if any, the Lakenheath post has to the enhanced force protection status. U.S. Air Forces in Europe – Air Forces Africa (USAFE) declined to discuss security measures. The command oversees U.S. Air Force operations in Europe and Africa.
“U.S. Air Force aircraft rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirements,” USAFE told us. “U.S. military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our Allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets.”
The departures from Mildenhall took place amid an ongoing flow of refueling tankers and other aircraft to the Middle East as President Donald Trump continues to mull whether to resume strikes against Iran . This afternoon, Trump wrapped up his meeting with Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani to discuss a flagging effort to resolve the conflict with Iran through diplomacy.
It should also be noted that in late November 2024, Lakenheath, Mildenhall and two other RAF bases hosting U.S. forces experienced drone incursions, which we were the first to write about .
As we mentioned earlier in this piece, security concerns about bases in England hosting U.S. Air Force aircraft and personnel were raised following an incident at RAF Fairford.
Like Mildenhall and Lakenheath, RAF Fairford is a major hub for U.S. military aircraft in the United Kingdom. It is a regular host of strategic assets, including bombers and U-2 spy planes. It also acts as a pit stop for other aircraft, including fighters, that are being ferried to and from the United States. Bomber strikes launched from Fairford were a central aspect of major U.S. combat operations against Iran earlier this year.
In late September, five men were arrested on suspicion of driving bomb-laden vans toward it. They were soon released on bail after no explosives were found, but two men were later arrested, one of who was “charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police earlier said they believed to be Iran,” according to the BBC .
A week after the security incident , U.S. Air Force B-1B Lancer bombers that had been deployed to RAF Fairford in the U.K. since Operation Epic Fury returned to their home stations, a U.S. defense official confirmed to TWZ at the time. The hasty movement was reportedly sparked by new Iranian threats against the base. As we previously reported , Tehran directly threatened RAF Fairford in July over its use as a base to launch attacks against Iran.
We can’t say for sure what prompted the enhanced security at RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall or whether the aircraft movements at Mildenhall are precautionary or just normal shifting of resources. We will continue to monitor the situation and provide updates when warranted.

articles.content_orig:
Boeing said Monday that it plans to cut 5% of its commercial airplane workforce as its production ramp-up is moving at a slower pace than the company expected.
The cuts will be through a combination of attrition and layoffs, Stephanie Pope, head of the commercial aircraft unit, said in a memo to staff.
Pope reiterated that the company is still working to stabilize production rates of its bestselling 737 Max planes, which are made outside of Seattle.
CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors last month that the company won't significantly increase production of the Max aircraft until the second half of next year. He said the company's wing production has been slower than expected.
"Adjusting our production schedules and reducing aircraft output puts us in an overstaffed position," Pope said in her note Monday. "Unfortunately, that means we need to align our staffing levels to our revised business plan, resulting in a reduction of approximately 5% through a combination of attrition and involuntary layoffs, with notifications beginning in December."
Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. Ortberg said the company has been trying to stabilize output at a rate of about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.

articles.title_orig: France accuses Iran of cyber 'sabotage' in fridge attacks
articles.title_zh: France accuses Iran of cyber 'sabotage' in fridge attacks
articles.content_orig:
A woman walks past empty refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, western France, on Oct. 12, following a cyberattack affecting the French supermarket chains Intermarché and Cooperative U that caused their refrigerators to defrost. FRED TANNEAU/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
France is accusing Iran of having launched a series of destructive cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure in October.
According to the French National Cybersecurity Agency, ANSSI, Iranian military hackers took over refrigeration controllers at around 700 different retail sites in France, from supermarkets to butcher shops, turning up the temperature in the middle of the night and spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food.
They also targeted several small hydroelectric power plants, resulting in "moderate effects," wrote ANSSI in its press release.
The hacking campaign was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," said French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot. He said it "marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people."
The Paris Prosecutor's Office has opened its own investigation into the Iranian cyber unit, Shahid Kaveh, which the French government is linking to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. "The Paris Public Prosecutor's Office is requesting the issuance of international arrest warrants," the office said in a statement.
The attacks on French industrial controllers are part of a larger trend . In 2026 alone, hackers have targeted refrigeration controllers from Europe to Israel and the United States.
Grocery stores in European countries including Sweden and Ireland were hit in similar attacks last week.
In a separate incident in France, employees at a major French blood bank had to act fast to save blood samples from heating up when their refrigeration system was hit last week, prompting international calls for the health sector to protect its lifesaving products from spoiling.
In Israel in the spring, suspected Iranian hackers going by the name of "Cyber Isnaad Front" claimed responsibility for sabotaging an industrial food processing plant, including infecting its corporate computers with malware, taking over office printers to print out threatening messages and hacking office cameras for use in a propaganda video released in early October. That video included a taunt in French referencing ongoing education-related protests, and came just before the attacks on French supermarket fridges. Cyber incident response firm Profero attributed the Israel attack to a wing of Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps .
Over the summer, commissaries on U.S. military bases also went through something similar, when food spoiled after the temperature shot up inside refrigerators and freezers overnight.
The French government is the first to formally assign blame for the wave of destructive attacks.
They were able to identify the hackers through a series of digital clues, including digital infrastructure used by the hackers, connection to a propaganda outlet, and "traces" of the use of Farsi language in the attack, according to ANSSI .
While NPR and others have reported that U.S. officials suspect Iran may have been behind the attacks on U.S. military bases in August, the Pentagon has not made any official statement, even to conclude that the disruptions were in fact the result of a cyberattack.
"Consistent with our policy and to preserve the integrity of the process, the DOD [Office of Inspector General] Criminal Investigative Service does not discuss ongoing investigations," Mollie Halpern, a spokesperson for the Department of War Office of the Inspector General wrote in an email to NPR.
If Iranian hackers are behind the attacks across Europe, the U.S. and Israel, cybersecurity experts say that would fit with what they know about Iranian hackers' strategy and goals.
"Iran's cyberattacks against refrigeration systems likely represents the IRGC attempting to reassert Iranian power abroad through both physically and psychologically disruptive operations," Alex Orleans, the head of threat intelligence at cybersecurity firm Sublime Security, told NPR. "Such activities continue to provide tangible and cost-effect results given how Iran's national resources remain tied down in the war."
"Also, Shahid Kaveh, the IRGC cyber unit that the French specifically attributed the disruptive attacks to, is repeating a pattern here," Orleans says. He referenced a series of cyberattacks on American water treatment plants in August, which most experts believe were linked to Iran, as precedent. The U.S. government has still not officially attributed those attacks.
"This unit has once again refined its tradecraft through attacks on Israeli targets before shifting their targeting to the same systems in the West," Orleans says.
For those tracking Shahid Kaveh and the other Iranian cyber units that operate alongside it, these attacks fit squarely into their modus operandi.
"Shahid Kaveh group is an offensive cyber unit responsible for some of the greatest hits of Iranian offensive cyber [operations]," says Ari Ben Am, an adjunct fellow at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies' Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation.
One group tied to Shahid Kaveh is the Cyber Av3ngers, he explains, which the U.S. government linked to cyberattacks on Israeli-made systems in U.S. water treatment facilities in the winter between 2023 and 2024. The French government also cited other cyberattacks carried out on behalf of the IRGC against French interests, including against the satirical French magazine Charlie Hebdo and another against digital kiosks used at the Paris Olympics in 2024.
Cybersecurity experts say the attacks on refrigeration controllers have highlighted a yearslong difficulty with securing operational technology, the machines that control physical processes in the real world — from water pumps to cooling systems.
These machines are often outdated and riddled with vulnerabilities, and are very difficult to patch because operators can't afford to shut them down and disrupt critical services including healthcare and transportation. Additionally, the machines are often left exposed to the open internet — often at least in part due to contractual requirements with vendors that want to maintain those systems remotely. That combination of factors makes it a complicated problem to solve .
Iran has yet to respond to the accusations. However, Monday's accusation by the French government may lead other affected countries to take action as well.
During Monday's G7 meeting in Paris, Secretary of State Marco Rubio was asked by journalists whether the U.S. shared information with the French to help with their attribution of the Iranian hacks. Rubio said he couldn't comment, but noted that the "French are quite capable."
"What kind of sickos are these people?" he asked. "They attack refrigerators. France is not even involved in this, really," referring to the war between the U.S. and Iran, which began in February. "[These Iranians] do terrible things around the world … the news today doesn't surprise us," Rubio concluded.
Rebecca Rosman reported from Paris.

articles.title_orig: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
articles.title_zh: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
articles.content_orig:
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.
Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.
In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.
The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.
"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.
Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.
It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.
The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.
But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.
For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.
"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.
It think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.
The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.
We don't know when their affair began or ended , but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.
China denies that she was engaged in espionage.
Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.
China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.
Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.
Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.
He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.
Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.
At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.
Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.
An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.
And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.
Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.
He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.
While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.
And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.
